beats.script_body: Travelers who need a break from the bustle of New York can escape to the Rubin, a serene museum of art from the Himalayas. Secular in origin — it was founded by an American millionaire and his wife who fell in love with the art of the region — its effect is nonetheless tremendously spiritual. The paintings, drawings, sculptures, and artifacts are all religious items, many used by traveling monks to teach Buddhism or to help worshippers deepen their meditation. That is why so many of the works are done on fabric: they were meant to be rolled up and carried. Many tell the stories of the various Buddhas, portraying meditating men with halos, snarling demons, teachers, and commoners in the deepest blues, ruby reds, emerald greens, and dazzling golds.

beats.script_body: At 28 acres, Hudson Yards is the largest private real estate development in American history — and amazingly, it was built in the most crowded city in the United States without displacing a single resident. The area it occupies, from 30th Street to 35th Street and Tenth Avenue to the river, covers the rail yards extending from Penn Station. An extraordinary feat of engineering created a platform above some 30 active railway tracks, with the massive skyscrapers resting partially on that platform and partially on caissons drilled into Manhattan's bedrock. The platform is wired with communication cables; rainwater from rooftops is filtered for on-site irrigation and drinking; and cooling units keep the heat of the train yards from affecting the 28,000 trees, grasses, wildflowers, and other plants in the park areas.

beats.script_body: For all its state-of-the-art innovations, Hudson Yards is one of the most unpopular projects in recent New York memory. Many locals compare it unfavorably with Rockefeller Center, the city's last large-scale development and a place of unparalleled architectural harmony. Unlike that project, which had a team of architects and designers working in tandem, Hudson Yards is simply a cluster of unrelated skyscrapers created by half a dozen different firms. The often-sneaky use of public funds to underwrite this private luxury development has also been galling to many New Yorkers.

beats.script_body: In ancient Roman times, the entrances to great cities were framed with monumental arches meant to awe all who passed through. When Grand Central Terminal was built at the turn of the last century, its architects recognized that railroad terminals were the city's grand gateways, and filled them with the symbols of imperial Rome. On Grand Central's south facade, 10 colossal Doric fluted pillars tower over Park Avenue; above them, a massive statue of Mercury, the god of travel, spreads his arms in welcome as Hercules and Minerva, gods of strength and wisdom, lounge at his feet. The face of the clock below the sculpture is the largest piece of Tiffany glass in the world.

Massive windows throw shafts of light onto the acre-long Tennessee marble floor. One of the station's innovations was the use of electric lights, so you'll see bare bulbs sprinkled throughout the station and on the massive chandeliers that overhang the concourse. Two hundred buildings were demolished to make way for the station, which opened on February 2, 1913, bearing a price tag of $80 million.

beats.script_body: The Morgan contains examples of the written word from the beginning of recorded time — from pictorial Mesopotamian cylinder seals of the 4th millennium B.C., to papyrus rolls from ancient Egypt, Greece, and Rome, to brilliantly colorful medieval illuminated manuscripts. Its crowning jewels are three editions of the Gutenberg Bible, the first book created using movable type. This is the only collection in the world to boast three editions; scholars come from around the globe to study them, as each is unique. Also in the collection are manuscripts by Mark Twain, Jane Austen, Charles Dickens, the Brontë sisters, Galileo, Bob Dylan, and James Joyce, one of 25 known surviving copies of the Declaration of Independence, and a First Folio of Shakespeare.

beats.script_body: Can an observation deck be a work of art? That's the provocative question developer SL Green Realty posed when it hired artist Kenzo Digital to create an immersive experience atop its newest skyscraper. Set right on 42nd Street, Summit One has heart-of-the-action views like the Empire State Building's, with even better views of the Chrysler Building since it's just a few buildings over. Those views are amplified and fractured by mirrors covering most of this 1,750,212-square-foot space — and the floors are mirrored too. Other surprises include three fully transparent “sky boxes” jutting from the side of the building, letting brave visitors stare down 1,063 feet to the sidewalk, a room with floating mirrored orbs, and a digital screen that transposes visitors' faces onto clouds.
